Require means: something is necessary — it cannot be skipped, ignored, or avoided.

When you say something is "required," you are saying its absence causes a real problem. Either a task fails, a rule is broken, or survival is impossible without it. It is not a preference or a suggestion. It is a genuine necessity.
The Two Main Ways It's Used

1. Natural or Practical Necessity

Here, "require" describes what something needs in order to function, exist, or succeed. No person is demanding anything — the situation itself makes it necessary.

"Plants require sunlight."
(Without sunlight, they simply cannot survive.)

"This recipe requires three eggs."
(Without the eggs, the recipe won't work.)

"Climbing this mountain requires great physical fitness."
(You cannot do it without that fitness.)

Notice: the subject (plants, the recipe, climbing the mountain) is not a person giving orders. It's a situation, a task, or a living thing. The necessity comes from the nature of things, not from someone's will.

2. Obligation Imposed by Authority, Rules, or Law

Here, "require" describes what a person, institution, law, or rule demands — something you are obligated to do or provide. Someone with authority is insisting on it.

"The law requires all drivers to carry a licence."
(It is a legal obligation. You have no choice.)

"The school requires students to wear uniforms."
(The institution is imposing this rule.)

"The contract requires payment within 30 days."
(A legal agreement is binding you to this.)

"My boss requires a weekly progress report from me."
(A person in authority is demanding this.)

Notice: the subject here is an authority — a law, an institution, a contract, a person in power. The necessity comes from their rules or demands.
The Crucial Shared Thread

Both uses share one thing: what is required is not optional.

  • In the first use — it's not optional because reality makes it impossible without it.
  • In the second use — it's not optional because breaking the rule has consequences (punishment, failure, legal trouble).

This is what makes "require" stronger and more serious than many other words.
Who or What Can "Require" Something?

Almost anything can be the subject of "require":

  • A task or activity: "The job requires five years of experience."
  • A place or institution: "The hospital requires visitors to register."
  • A situation: "The crisis requires immediate attention."
  • A law or rule: "The regulation requires safety helmets on the site."
  • A formal/official person: "The judge requires your presence in court."
  • A living thing: "The human body requires sleep."
How to Use It in a Sentence (Grammar Patterns)

Pattern 1: require + noun

"This work requires patience."
"The task requires complete silence."

Pattern 2: require + object + to + verb
(Someone requires a person to do something)

"The manager requires all staff to sign in."
"The form requires you to provide your address."

Pattern 3: require + that + clause (more formal)

"The rules require that all phones be switched off."
"The policy requires that employees declare any conflicts."

Pattern 4: require + verb-ing

"The project requires testing every component."
"The job requires travelling frequently."
"Required" — the Adjective Form

When something is described as "required," it means it is compulsory or necessary — not optional.

"Attendance is required." (You must attend.)
"A signature is required." (You must sign.)
"These are the required documents." (You must have these.)
How "Require" Compares to Similar Words

Understanding where "require" sits among similar words sharpens your sense of it greatly.

Require vs. Want
"Want" is a desire — you can live without it. "Require" is a necessity — you cannot proceed without it.

"I want a bigger office." (desire, optional)
"The machine requires a power source." (necessity, non-negotiable)

Require vs. Need
These are very close in meaning. The key difference is tone. "Need" is neutral and everyday. "Require" is more formal, more precise, and often carries a sense of authority or structure.

"I need help." (casual, personal)
"The process requires authorisation from two managers." (formal, procedural)

Require vs. Request
A "request" is an asking — the other person can say no. "Require" is a necessity or demand — there is no real option to decline.

"I request your feedback." (polite asking; you may choose)
"The visa requires a bank statement." (you must provide it; there is no option)

Require vs. Demand
Both involve insisting, but "demand" is more aggressive and emotional — it often implies impatience or confrontation. "Require" is more formal and neutral — it describes a rule, a system, a law, or a calm authority.

"He demanded an apology." (forceful, emotional, personal)
"The application requires proof of identity." (formal, impersonal, structured)
The Passive Voice: "Required to"

You will very often see "require" used in the passive form: "is/are required to." This is extremely common in formal, legal, and official language.

"You are required to submit your documents by Monday."
"All passengers are required to fasten their seatbelts."
"Employees are required to complete the training."

This passive form puts the focus on the obligation itself, not on who is imposing it. It sounds official and impersonal — like a rule that exists above any individual.
Subtle Nuance: Require Implies Genuine Necessity

There is an important subtlety. "Require" implies that if the required thing is absent, something genuinely goes wrong — not just inconveniently, but fundamentally.

"Success requires hard work."

This doesn't mean hard work is merely helpful. It means without hard work, success is not fully possible.

"The job requires a degree."

This means without the degree, you are disqualified — not just disadvantaged.

This sense of genuine, non-trivial necessity is what gives "require" its weight and seriousness.
A Few More Natural Examples in Context

• "Good writing requires clarity of thought." — clarity is a true necessity for good writing.
  • "The experiment requires precise measurements." — without precision, the experiment is compromised.
  • "Your visa requires a valid passport." — no passport, no visa. Full stop.
  • "Running a business requires both skill and patience." — both are genuinely needed, not just helpful.
  • "The position requires fluency in two languages." — it is a mandatory condition of the role.
  • "The medicine requires a doctor's prescription." — you legally cannot get it without one.
Summary

Require means: something is a genuine necessity — it must be present or done, and its absence leads to failure, impossibility, or violation of a rule. It is used both when nature/reality makes something necessary, and when a rule, law, or authority imposes an obligation. It is more formal than "need," stronger than "want," calmer than "demand," and more binding than "request." What is required is never optional.
